XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated: 1. Will the First Minister provide an update on the Welsh Government's position on the Global Centre of Rail Excellence? OQ64526

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: The question does indeed come at an opportune time. A review has been commissioned, looking at how to deliver the best outcome at the Nant Helen site. We are keen now to develop a clear direction of travel with GCRE Ltd.

Thank you for that update, First Minister. The Economy, Trade and Rural Affairs Committee in the last session visited the site and looked into the proposals that were presented to us. When this concept was first thought through, there was the potential for 1,000 jobs coming to the site, and the Government of the day was told that there was huge demand for this testing facility. Regrettably, to date, not £1 of private money has gone into it. It is a huge site. I saw a media report saying it's the size of Gibraltar. There's a lot of remediation work to go into it. The one thing we were told as a committee was that the incoming Government, whoever that Government would be, needed to make a quick decision about future investment. The site has burned through £70 million of public money to date. When will you be in the position to formulate what the Government is going to do, bearing in mind £70 million of public money has already gone in and £350 to £400 million is required to build this Global Centre of Rail Excellence?

Llywydd, the Member makes very important points. Significant amounts of public funding have gone into the site already. I'm not going to criticise the concept that came from the current leader of the Labour Party, but we have to understand what has happened as those tens of millions of pounds have been spent on the site, and what maybe hasn't happened to enable us to be at a place where there is private funding willing and able and keen to come in. As I say, my Minister has commissioned that work now because I agree that we need to come to a decision soon in order to make the most of the opportunities for what is still a very important site.

First Minister, it's good to hear that you are commissioning a review, but this Chamber would like to understand that the confidence of your Government in this site must rest on a credible commercial case, which the public actually needs to understand. The additional proposed data centre and energy park may promise local jobs, but these benefits cannot justify an indefinite dependence on taxpayer-funded grants. After more than four months in office, your Government should be able to demonstrate how and when the development will attract private capital and generate a sufficient income to support itself. How will you make any further development conditional on a financially self-supporting business plan that delivers measurable local benefits without further taxpayer-funded grants to GCRE or participating companies? Thank you.

Again, perfectly appropriate questions to ask. It is not just about making it a credible commercial proposition, it's making sure that the public money that has gone into it has been put to good use, and, as we consider the future, that we look at that balance of where Government works potentially with the private sector on what could be a whole host of different propositions. As I say, the fact that we understand the need to move quickly on this is why that review has been commissioned. Whatever the project, you cannot continue to move forward in an aimless way. This started from a point where there was a real belief in a particular project. Time has moved on. We need to make sure that, in 2026, we understand what the best project is now for that site.

The Global Centre of Rail Excellence is seen as a promising development for many across my constituency, showing the potential of green travel, a path towards net zero, and supporting the development of stronger, greener and more affordable transport systems right across the world. What other opportunities are there alongside this project that will help people in my constituency? Diolch.

The Member again points to that original concept around rail. A lot has happened in rail since those times, not least the changes in direction around HS2 and so on. We need to understand where we are now, rather than where we were. We need to understand the significance of decisions that have been made to date. The Member will want to ensure that what we achieve there is something that is of value to the locality, to the constituency that she and others represent, and to the Welsh economy. And those are the principles that will be guiding my Cabinet Minister for enterprise as he now works with the review and looks forward to seeing the results of that review pretty soon.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: 2. Beth yw blaenoriaethau gofal iechyd Llywodraeth Cymru ar gyfer Ceredigion Penfro ar gyfer y deuddeg mis nesaf? OQ64479
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated: 2. What are the Welsh Government's healthcare priorities for Ceredigion Penfro for the next twelve months? OQ64479

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: Improving health outcomes, ensuring timely access to care, supporting sustainable NHS services for communities across Ceredigion Penfro are clearly major priorities for this new Government. As part of our vision to strengthen healthcare in rural and coastal areas in particular, we will engage closely with the local health board and partners to ensure high-quality, patient-centred services that genuinely do meet the needs of local people. We want to make sure they're delivered now and into the future.

First Minister, I believe that the Welsh Government's healthcare priorities for Ceredigion Penfro must be to protect essential health services at its hospitals so that patients do not have to travel further afield for treatment. Now, over the years, my constituents have seen health services centralised and moved further away by the local health board, despite clear public opposition to these changes. And there has been little, if any, intervention or challenge from a Welsh Government over the last 27 years. Now, following the change of Government in May, there was a sense of hope for my constituents that their views would be heard and the health board stopped, and, so far, that has not been the case. So, First Minister, what threshold must be crossed before the Welsh Government is prepared to intervene and prevent Hywel Dda University Health Board from further downgrading services in west Wales? And what message do you have for the people of Ceredigion Penfro who voted for a Government they believed would stand up for local communities and ensure that no further services are removed from their hospitals?

Llywydd, the Member is absolutely right that we want to protect essential services, and most of us at one time or another have been involved in various campaigns around particular services in different places. I think the principles that we need to bear in mind always are that we provide timely services in the appropriate location. There will be different stories in different parts of Wales, but those are the principles that tie us together.

Decisions on clinical services are taken by the health boards themselves. I know that the health board in this particular instance has looked at eight out of nine of the services that it provides and consulted on them, and put in place changes that it believes would provide better services to be delivered over the best part of a decade. These aren't overnight changes. And it's important to remember that these are changes that can take time. But my appeal always is for health boards, when they make those changes, when they consult, and afterwards, to ensure that people feel that they are engaged properly on those decisions. But there will be, clearly, different applications of different services in different parts of Wales. It's about getting that balance of appropriate services that will always put the patient first.

Thank you to Paul Davies for the question. First Minister, 35 per cent of Ceredigion households and 23 per cent in Pembrokeshire rely on oil heating, among the highest rates in Wales. Public Health Wales warns that cold homes increase cardiovascular and respiratory risks, particular for older and vulnerable people. As your Government moves towards net zero, how will you ensure that rural households are not forced to ration heating because of the cost of that transition, and will you guarantee that keeping people warm and healthy comes before hitting arbitrary deadlines? Diolch.

I will accept that there is a healthcare link there, Llywydd, and I'm being very, very generous. We know that a healthy home, a healthy environment, is important for people's health, so the Member is absolutely right in that respect.

On oil heating in particular, of course, these are measures that are reserved. We have consistently appealed to the UK Government to make the right decisions when it comes to the options that it has at its disposal, but that we haven't as a Welsh Government, to relieve the pressure on households in rural Wales in particular that are particularly dependent on off-grid oil. It is a principle that ties this Government together, that we think cross-departmentally, and the Member is right: we need to think housing, we need to think energy, we need to think health when it comes to the well-being of the people that we represent.

First Minister, I'd like to agree that protecting services at Bronglais and Withybush hospitals remains vital for communities across Ceredigion Penfro. However, in rural areas, we also need innovative ways of bringing healthcare closer to people's homes. Integrated care centres in Cardigan and Aberaeron show what can be achieved when we bring services together, and, again, bring them closer to people, taking the pressure off hospitals. Having recently visited GP services in Fishguard, I know that there is strong local support for a similar approach there. Indeed, my colleague Elin Jones has previously worked with local councillors to make the case for an integrated care centre for Fishguard. So, will the Welsh Government commit to working with Hywel Dda University Health Board and local communities to explore how towns such as Fishguard could benefit from integrated care facilities, ensuring rural communities are not left behind as healthcare services evolve?

Many of us represent rural areas here, and the health of somebody in a rural part of Wales is as important as somebody in an urban part of Wales. We need to make sure that we have equitable healthcare, but it does mean that a different approach is needed. I'm really interested in the work that is developing—already has begun—into creating a centre of excellence on the delivery of rural healthcare in Bronglais Hospital, which could benefit all parts of Wales, not just Ceredigion Penfro.

The programme for government commitment is clear. We want to ensure that integrated care is delivered closer to home, with prevention in particular at its core, to support earlier diagnosis, reduce admissions and delays in discharge. We have many ideas on how, in general, the delivery can be improved in rural areas, but health officials, I know, are engaging with the health board and Pembrokeshire County Council specifically on the development of that integrated centre in Fishguard.

First Minister, making sure victims' voices are heard—that is not political point scoring.

What I admire is that somebody would have the bravery to stand up to this Reform group in the Senedd and say, 'I now can see you for what you are.' 'Yes' or 'no'? Okay. Diolch yn fawr.

First Minister, today we remember the deaths of hundreds of people in the Gresford mining disaster. It was a horrific disaster that devastated the community, and I'm sure you, First Minister, will also remember those who died. More than 260 bodies were recovered, but 253 remain entombed. Let me, firstly, associate myself very much with the comments as we remember the Gresford disaster, and we send our thoughts to the community, for whom the pain of that day is still felt in many ways.

First Minister, the £9 million that you refer to was before the UK Government budget. I ask the Member to look again at when they were promising £9 million, and it was very much after that money was made available. And there are principles here about the ability for us to set directions here in Wales. I am familiar with Clwb Cwtsh. That money includes money that would directly go to Flintshire council, so I'm imagining that the leader of Flintshire council would be keen for the Labour leader here to help us get that money out of the door.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: 3. Beth mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn ei wneud i baratoi ar gyfer digwyddiadau tywydd garw ac eithafol y gaeaf hwn? OQ64508
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated: 3. What is the Welsh Government doing to prepare for adverse and extreme weather events this winter? OQ64508

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: I know the Member agrees with me that the evidence is clear: climate change is increasing the frequency and intensity of extreme weather. We are committed to building stronger, more resilient communities across Wales in that changing context. We're working closely with partners, including through the Wales resilience forum and local resilience forums to prepare for winter risks, to strengthen response arrangements and learn from recent extreme weather events. We're also making communities more resilient to flooding through continued investment in infrastructure and nature-based solutions.

Thank you. Last week, First Minister, you issued a statement saying that you will convene a resilience summit focusing on wildfires—very much welcomed. Yet, we must be ready for all of the escalating risks of a changing climate. This includes extreme cold, winter flooding and severe storms this coming winter. The Met Office has warned of a heightened risk on the horizon due to an unprecedented El Niño event this year, only highlighted in shocking headlines yesterday, recording the record breaking of 150 years of records. Weaknesses in our infrastructure and our resilience, such as recently witnessed in Gwaelod-y-garth, will only become more apparent in the coming months.

Wales is dangerously unprepared for the predicted onslaught of extreme weather conditions. Climate response must be integrated as our first line of defence. Welsh Government allocated in its supplementary budget just £1 million for emergency preparedness. Establishing a climate shock fund would be a vital step forward in demonstrating that the Welsh Government is serious about protecting communities this winter, with or without UK Government support. What discussions has the First Minister had with the UK Government on funding these emergency measures? Diolch.

Thank you for the question. I think the world is largely unprepared for the challenges that we face. The question is how can we accelerate our preparedness. You will see in the programme for government today that climate change isn't seen as a priority in and of itself; it's one of the priorities that binds us all together as Government Ministers, because this has to be addressed across all portfolios.

Resilience—I talked about this last week—is an issue that I have tried to focus a great deal on since I came into the role of First Minister, understanding the various elements that contribute to the resilience, or lack of, in some ways, that we have as a society. Wildfires happen to be the one that has grabbed our attention, which is why we need to make sure that we're tightening up those resilience elements around that in the summit on 22 October. But the Member is right; flooding is something that many communities will be concerned about. There are other concerns too—the effects of heat, the effects of cold and so on.

I thank her for that further question, but the truth is that the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care has been very clear that any proposals for service change must be informed by evidence and with full regard to quality, safety and patient experience. Those powers, clearly, are to safeguard patients and are intended to address significant patient safety concerns, failures in consultation or decision making, breaches of statutory duties or wider governance concerns. Therefore, with respect, political opposition, public concern or the controversial nature of a proposal would not, of itself, ordinarily justify intervention. These powers are safeguards for addressing failures by local health boards in discharge of functions and they are not a mechanism for reconsidering the merits or demerits of any clinical service decision. XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
Well, of course, the role of Welsh Government is to defend the devolution settlement, but also to ensure that things such as the Sewel convention are observed, and to defend and extend the relationship, one hopes.

In July of this year, I published the Welsh Government's principles on UK legislation in devolved areas, and this includes a commitment that the UK legislation in devolved areas will only be used where the legislation protects or strengthens the devolution settlement and does not introduce new constraints on devolved competence. And I am very clear, as is this Government, that we are focused on enhancing the devolution settlement, and with that, the Senedd’s legislative competence, rather than simply maintaining it. However, where there are attempts to limit or constrain the Senedd’s legislative competence, these will be firmly resisted, and this includes opposing the imposition of any further reservations or restrictions in the Government of Wales Act 2006, as well as securing relevant consents and carve-outs to ensure that devolved provisions conferred by UK parliamentary Acts can be removed by the Senedd at a later date. And I think key to all of this is the principle of legislative consent as set out clearly in the Sewel convention. This is essential to our devolution settlement and safeguards the Senedd’s role as the Welsh national legislature. As Counsel General, I am clear that the Sewel convention must be respected, particularly where there are any attempts to reduce or restrict the Senedd’s legislative competence via UK legislation.

Now, the Government's view is we would like it to have statutory underpinning. That is not forthcoming at the moment. There are discussions going on. Meantime, what is currently happening is there's a detailed discussion about a firm, proper solid memorandum of understanding on Sewel. It's probably second-best to having it on a statutory footing, but it is being

but it is being undertaken and discussed as we speak now. So, something is happening. But I fully appreciate the force of the question. It is vital that we ensure that Sewel is respected, as it has been disrespected so often of late.

Counsel General, I'm sure that, as a former Member of Parliament, the Counsel General is well acquainted with the concept of parliamentary sovereignty. Of course, access to justice means more than just access to the courts. People must understand their rights and get reliable advice at the right time and participate effectively in legal processes that have an impact upon them. And the ability to use the Welsh language in legal cases is an important principle within the justice system in Wales. And arrangements are in place to support Welsh-medium cases, including interpretation, translation and bilingual documentation as necessary.

Wales, of course, is a bilingual nation, but in asking what specifically can be done, this is now a very live issue; it is an issue that will be raised in various conferences over this winter. So, there is a great job of work to be done, and it is part of my job description to ensure that access to the law is possible through the medium of both languages. And it's something that's at the forefront of my mind and something that I will be working on in the coming months.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: My question has some crossover with the question that Mike Hedges asked earlier.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated: 6. What assessment has the Counsel General made of the impact of pressures on legal aid provision on access to justice in Wales? OQ64498

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: Pressures on legal aid provision in Wales are a very serious concern. Reduced provision means many communities cannot access the legal help they need. Although legal aid is reserved to the UK Government, we will always look for opportunities to bring these problems to the attention of the Ministry of Justice.

Diolch yn fawr iawn. We know how vital legal aid is to helping those in need and ensuring that everybody has the right to adequate legal representation. A report by the House of Lords select committee last year concluded that there are people who are both unable to access legal aid and unable to afford to pay for legal services privately. As the Law Society have noted, proposals put forward by the UK Government have not addressed the distinct issues facing the legal sector in Wales and that the part or full devolution of justice, if implemented and funded appropriately, offers significant potential opportunities to the people of Wales. What advice has the Counsel General given the Welsh Government on the adequacy of legal aid in Wales?

Well, it is a matter that the Welsh Government are acutely aware of, and it's partly because of the narrowing of the scope of legal aid alongside tighter eligibility criteria. That's had a very significant impact over many years on the justice system across England and Wales. I'm particularly concerned that people in many parts of Wales are unable to access local legal advice because legal aid fees are no longer sufficient to support sustainable provision. In Wales, reduced provision has contributed to legal advice deserts, leaving some communities without local access to specialist legal help. For example, the Law Society's heat maps show that 82 per cent of the people of Wales have no access to a legal aid-funded local welfare provider, and no less than 88 per cent have no education law provider.

These pressures are acute everywhere, but particularly so in rural, post-industrial and lower income communities, similar to the area that the Member represents. Where alternative sources of advice may be very limited, and without early legal advice, problems can escalate, increasing pressures on devolved services including health, housing and social care. Through the regional advice networks, we are supporting closer collaboration between private law firms and not-for-profit advice providers so that people across Wales can access the advice they need. Although, as I've said before, legal aid is reserved, we will work closely with the Ministry of Justice, the UK Government and legal professions in Wales to ensure Wales's needs are clearly understood and are reflected in the response to these pressures.

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated: Access to Justice for Rape Survivors

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim: 8. Sut mae'r Cwnsler Cyffredinol yn hyrwyddo mynediad at gyfiawnder i oroeswyr treisio? OQ64490
XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_translated: 8. How is the Counsel General promoting access to justice for rape survivors? OQ64490

XML_Plenary_Bilingual.contribution_verbatim:
While criminal justice, as the Member knows, is largely reserved, the Welsh Government works with policing, the Crown Prosecution Service, courts and specialist services to improve access to justice for rape survivors. Through the violence against women, domestic abuse and sexual violence agenda, we fund advocacy, counselling and support services, including independent sexual violence advisers, helping survivors access information, support and justice.

I would further say that the Government has invested in specialist support services throughout the piece. More needs to be done, I hasten to add, and we recognise that access to justice is about more than court outcomes. Survivors must be able to access timely support, information and advocacy so they can make informed decisions and recover from the impact of abuse.

And with regard to the university sector, all learners, including university students, should be able to study in safe environments free from violence, abuse, harassment and intimidation. Whilst universities in Wales are autonomous, we expect them to take robust action to ensure safe and supportive teaching environments. Medr's new staff and learner welfare condition has introduced clearer expectations on well-being, safety and protection from harassment and misconduct, including sexual violence. Officials are working closely with Medr and universities and sector partners to strengthen prevention, reporting and support, improve consistency and transparency, support providers to create safe cultures where concerns are taken seriously. I would suggest to the Member that she writes to my colleague, the Deputy First Minister, on this matter, and I am sure that she will get a full and substantive response on the current steps being taken.

Thank you for that. I was pleased to see the UK Government announcement that specialist courts to deal with rape and sexual offences are to be introduced across England and Wales, and, hopefully, this begins to tackle the shamefully low prosecution rates of rape in the UK, which has effectively been decriminalised.

However, we also must look at prevention, not just justice. I met with a group of young women at Cardiff University, so I was glad to hear you talk about the university sector. They're called Time to Act, and they've been campaigning to eliminate sexual assault and sexual harassment from campuses, alongside supporting survivors. In England, as you'll know, there are currently regulatory consequences for institutions that fail to prevent and tackle harassment and sexual misconduct. Students in Wales don't have this equivalent protection, so I was wondering if you would, potentially, look at what avenues are available for the Welsh Government to legislate and prevent sexual harassment and violence on university campus.

Well, I hear what the Member says, and I appreciate the work that she's doing in the area. It's certainly very important, and I can speak from my own personal knowledge of work I do at the university in Aberystwyth. It's high on the agenda at that university and, I have no doubt, in every university in Wales, and so it should be. So, things are moving, albeit slower than all of us would want, but they are moving in the right direction. And our job, it seems to me, is to pressurise and ensure that the continued improvement in this area is to be seen by all.

to be seen by all.

If I add one final thing, on the issue of rape generally—horrific as it is—there has been an announcement that there will be, from 1 October, a designated court dealing with rape. That will lessen the backlog, and that will include specialists available to help and back up individuals but also things like separate entrances and waiting rooms, basic protections of that kind. This is something that I believe to be welcomed. I would also say, on a more positive note, the backlogs in Wales are considerably better than they are elsewhere in the UK, and we need to maintain that, but this, again, will assist, I belive.
